title: Raptor electrocution rates for a utility in the Intermountain Western United States
abstract: We estimated electrocution rates for raptors and common ravens (Corvus corax) for the Moon Lake Electrical Association in northeastern Utah and northwestern Colorado, USA. From July 2001 to May 2003, we conducted mortality searches at randomly selected distribution line segments and poles within 3 regions, but rate estimates (0.0036–0.0112 deaths/pole/yr) may have been biased by the effects of scavengers and by long sampling intervals ( 3 months), which prevented us from determining the cause of death for most birds because of advanced decay. In 2002–2003, we conducted carcass removal experiments in the Rangely Oil Field (ROF) in northwestern Colorado to estimate scavenging effects, and in 2003–2004, we reduced sampling intervals to 1 month and searched for dead birds at all distribution poles in the ROF. The shorter sampling interval nearly tripled the number of birds suitable for necropsy, but we were still unable to establish cause of death for .40% of our sample. Instead of eliminating the unknowns from rate estimates, we estimated minimum annual electrocution rates using only confirmed electrocutions and maximum annual electrocution rates based on all available mortalities, including mortalities without known causes. Golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) accounted for 63% of dead birds found in 2003–2004, but they were removed by scavengers at rates well below hawks and owls (6.8% vs. 55.6%). We compared maximum rates for the ROF in 2003–2004 with the rates estimated from a survey conducted at the same poles in 1999 to assess the effects of retrofitting conducted by Moon Lake from 1999 to 2003. Electrocution rates in 2003–2004 were 47% lower than those in 1999. Raptor densities in the ROF did not change during our study, suggesting the reduction was not the result of changes in raptor populations. However, estimates of raptor densities in 1999 were not available, and we cannot be sure that numbers of birds using the oil field in 1999 were similar to those in 2003–2004. Our research emphasizes the difficulties of estimating electrocution rates precisely but suggests that utilities will have the greatest effect on mortality by monitoring power lines at large scales and focusing subsequent mitigation efforts in areas that pose the greatest risk to the greatest number of birds.

## Management and Conservation Article

## Electrocution Rates for a Raptor Utility in the Intermountain Western United States

ROBERT N. LEHMAN,[1] 2023 South Ridge Point Way, Boise, ID 83712, USA

JULIE A. SAVIDGE, Colorado State University, Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Conservation Biology, Fort Collins, CO 80523, USA PATRICIA L. KENNEDY, Oregon State University, Eastern Oregon Agricultural Research Center and Department of Fisheries and Wildlife, P.O. Box E, Union, OR 97883, USA RICHARD E. HARNESS, EDM International, Inc., 4001 Automation Way, Fort Collins, CO 80525, USA

ABSTRACT We estimated electrocution rates for raptors and common ravens (Corvus corax) for the Moon Lake Electrical Association in northeastern Utah and northwestern Colorado, USA. From July 2001 to May 2003, we conducted mortality searches at randomly selected distribution line segments and poles within 3 regions, but rate estimates (0.0036–0.0112 deaths/pole/yr) may have been biased by the effects of scavengers and by long sampling intervals ( 3 months), which prevented us from determining the cause of death for most birds because of advanced decay. In 2002–2003, we conducted carcass removal experiments in the Rangely Oil Field (ROF) in northwestern Colorado to estimate scavenging effects, and in 2003–2004, we reduced sampling intervals to 1 month and searched for dead birds at all distribution poles in the ROF. The shorter sampling interval nearly tripled the number of birds suitable for necropsy, but we were still unable to establish cause of death for .40% of our sample. Instead of eliminating the unknowns from rate estimates, we estimated minimum annual electrocution rates using only confirmed electrocutions and maximum annual electrocution rates based on all available mortalities, including mortalities without known causes. Golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) accounted for 63% of dead birds found in 2003–2004, but they were removed by scavengers at rates well below hawks and owls (6.8% vs. 55.6%). We compared maximum rates for the ROF in 2003–2004 with the rates estimated from a survey conducted at the same poles in 1999 to assess the effects of retrofitting conducted by Moon Lake from 1999 to 2003. Electrocution rates in 2003–2004 were 47% lower than those in 1999. Raptor densities in the ROF did not change during our study, suggesting the reduction was not the result of changes in raptor populations. However, estimates of raptor densities in 1999 were not available, and we cannot be sure that numbers of birds using the oil field in 1999 were similar to those in 2003–2004. Our research emphasizes the difficulties of estimating electrocution rates precisely but suggests that utilities will have the greatest effect on mortality by monitoring power lines at large scales and focusing subsequent mitigation efforts in areas that pose the greatest risk to the greatest number of birds.

KEY WORDS Aquila chrysaetos, Colorado, distance sampling, electrocution rates, golden eagle, necropsies, power lines, raptors, Utah.

Overhead power lines are a component of many wildlife habitats and concerns about electrocution of raptors and other birds on these facilities is increasing throughout the world (Bevanger 1998, Janss and Ferrer 1999a, Lehman 2001, Hunting 2002). Electrocutions (mortalities caused by electric current) are a consequence of the arrangement and spacing of energized and grounded components of poles and towers that raptors use for perching and other activities (Avian Power Line Interaction Committee [APLIC] 2006). In the United States, nearly all electrocutions occur on comparatively low-voltage distribution lines ( 69 kV) that supply residential and commercial customers, as opposed to transmission lines that transmit power at higher loads ( 115 kV) between distribution centers (APLIC 2006). Lower voltages require clearances between electrical components that often are smaller than the wingspans and other physical dimensions of many raptors. In the United States, .30 raptor species have been reported as electrocution mortalities, and worldwide .70 species have appeared in power-line mortality data (Hunting 2002). Electrocutions have been implicated as a cause of population declines in some species (e.g., Bonelli’s eagle [Hieraaetus fasciatus] and eagle owl [Bubo bubo] in western Europe; Real et al. 1996, Rubolini et al.

2001), and for others, they are a leading cause of death (e.g., the golden eagle [Aquila chrysaetos] in North America; Franson et al. 1995). Electrocutions can cause local and even regional service disruptions (i.e., power outages), equipment damage, forest and rangeland fires, safety problems, and lost productivity for consumers (Harness and Wilson 2001, APLIC 2006). The economic effects of the problem are not fully known, but power outages alone cost service providers, consumers, and business sectors billions of dollars annually, and avian and animal electrocutions are a major cause of these outages (12% by one estimate; Electric Power Research Institute 2001). In recent years, raptor electrocutions have led to increased scrutiny by regulatory and law enforcement agencies, negative media attention, and even criminal prosecutions of power companies (Melcher and Suazo 1999, Suazo 2000, Williams 2000). Yet, in spite of the need for effective management of electrocution risks, basic questions about raptor electrocutions, including some that are essential to treating the problem, remain unresolved. Numbers of birds electrocuted each year have been estimated only roughly in most regions of the world or have not been estimated (Lehman 2001). For example, in the United States, estimates of mortality have ranged from thousands to hundreds of thousands of deaths annually (Lehman 2001, Manville 2005).

In a recent review, Lehman et al. (2007) found that study design and sampling issues have limited the usefulness of many studies on raptor electrocution throughout the world. Nearly half of .100 studies analyzed for scientific merit and relevance were retrospective reviews of mortality records from industry or agency files or resulted from necropsies performed opportunistically at pathology and veterinary facilities. Mortality estimates from these studies were probably biased but to unknown degrees. Among prospective studies, ,50% used unbiased sampling protocols (e.g., randomized searches for dead birds), and most studies reported mortality as a raw count (i.e., no. of dead birds recorded) or as a simple rate (i.e., a function of time: deaths/ month or deaths/yr) or number of poles surveyed (deaths/ pole). Worldwide, only 6 studies reported mortality as a function of time and spatial scale (e.g., deaths/pole/yr) and only 5 studies reported mortality before and after retrofitting. Few studies evaluated how errors in assigning cause of death or scavenging of dead birds influenced mortality estimates, and fewer still considered how raptor density or abundance affected the number of birds killed.

Informed decision making in response to the raptor electrocution problem requires a basic understanding of how and why raptors interact with power lines and the factors that drive electrocution risk (see reviews by Hunting 2002, APLIC 2006, Lehman et al. 2007). Effective mitigation requires techniques that allow researchers to target and modify high-risk poles during large-scale retrofitting operations. Action at any scale, however, will be of limited practical value if monitoring and mitigation techniques and products used to correct hazardous poles are not scientifically evaluated. Estimates of mortality that incorporate temporal and spatial scales are important because they compensate for varying pole counts and survey effort among samples and are broadly applicable for contrasting mortality across studies, establishing baselines and monitoring trends, assessing effects, and evaluating management actions aimed at reducing electrocution risks. Ultimately, support for raptor protection programs and incentives for energy suppliers to undertake large-scale, expensive retrofitting operations will hinge on the availability of sound assessment tools and past successes.

We assess patterns of raptor and common raven (Corvus corax) mortality in areas served by the Moon Lake Electrical Association (hereafter, Moon Lake) in northwestern Colorado, and northeastern Utah, USA (Fig. 1). Our main goals were to 1) estimate and contrast electrocution rates among major landscape categories, pole types, and species groups; 2) evaluate potential biases in rate estimates and adjust estimates accordingly; and 3) contrast mortality before and after a retrofitting effort conducted by Moon Lake from 1999 to 2003. Secondary goals were to establish a basis for evaluating Moon Lake’s raptor protection efforts and to provide recommendations for improving mortality estimates and assessing the effectiveness of mitigation efforts at large scales. Goals relating to the first objective (rate estimates) were to evaluate 1-phase vs. 3-phase poles (i.e., poles with 1 vs. 3 conductors) and to assess electrocution rates among

Figure 1. Vicinity map of the Moon Lake Electrical Association service area, northeastern Utah and northwestern Colorado, USA, showing distribution line segments monitored for raptor mortalities during random sampling efforts in the Uintah Basin and High Desert (2001–2003).

species from different size classes. We expected electrocution rates to differ along taxonomic lines and predicted that rates for large-bodied raptors (eagles) would be higher than rates for smaller birds (e.g., falcons [Falco spp.], owls, buteos [Buteo spp.], and accipiters [Accipiter spp.]). We expected rates for 1-phase poles to be lower than those for 3-phase configurations.

## STUDY AREA

The Intermountain West is a region of arid and semiarid highlands bordered on the east by the Rocky Mountains and on the west by the Sierra Nevada and Cascade Mountains. The region is characterized by a dry climate, high elevations (.1,500 m in the study area), and isolated mountain ranges and mesas that rise from broad, flat, intermountain basins. Sagebrush (Artemisia spp.) and saltbush (Artemisia and Atriplex spp.) steppes dominate the lower mountain slopes and basins, giving way to pinyon–juniper (Pinus edulis and Juniperus spp.) and coniferous woodlands at higher elevations (Bailey 1995). A striking feature of many Intermountain West landscapes is the lack of trees, and as a result, power poles are often used by raptors for hunting, loafing, and roosting (Olendorff et al. 1981, APLIC 2006). Historically, the Intermountain West has supported important populations of raptors, including some of the largest populations of the golden eagle in North America

Figure 2. Typical distribution pole configurations in the Moon Lake study area, northeastern Utah and northwestern Colorado, USA (2001–2004), including 2 low-risk configurations (1-phase and 3-phase tangent poles) and 2 high-risk configurations (3-phase tap pole and 3-phase pole with pole-mounted equipment).

(Olendorff et al. 1981, Harlow and Bloom 1989). Golden eagles have appeared in power-line mortality records from this region more than any other species, and electrocutions may be an important limiting factor for the species (Boeker and Nickerson 1975, Nelson and Nelson 1976, Benson 1981, Harness and Wilson 2001). Migration counts and Christmas Bird Counts suggest golden eagle populations have declined in western North America since the early 1980s with accelerating declines since 1998 (Farmer et al. 2008).

Our study area encompassed 19,030 km[2] of the northern Colorado Plateau, roughly comprising the Green River and its drainages. Within this area, Moon Lake maintained transmission and distribution lines, substations, and other facilities to provide service to nearly 17,000 residential and commercial customers. Distribution networks included .55,000 poles, mostly constructed of wood and framed for operation at 7.2 kV with 1 phase (i.e., conductor) or 12.5–7.2 kV with 3 phases (Fig. 2). However, network design and function varied within 3 distinct regions (Fig. 1). The Rangely Oil Field (ROF), operated by Chevron Corporation in northwestern Colorado, encompassed just 85 km[2] (,1% of the study area) but had the most powerline mortalities recorded before our study (134 of 210 mortalities [64%]; K. Winder, Moon Lake Electrical Association, unpublished data). During our study, Moon Lake maintained approximately 2,930 distribution poles in

the ROF (5% of all poles), providing power to approximately 350 oil wells and other facilities (J. Roedell, Chevron Corporation, personal communication; Fig. 3). Because each well required transformers to reduce voltage and often a feeder line to provide power, the distribution system formed a concentrated network of power lines, had the highest pole densities in the study area, and had the largest proportion of poles in high-risk categories. High-risk structures included poles at line intersections (hereafter, taps), poles with transformers at delivery points (dead-end units), or any pole with specialized equipment (e.g., fused cutouts, jumper wires; Fig. 2). These pole types were particularly hazardous because the wiring needed to link energized and grounded components decreased clearances for birds, increasing the risk of electrocution (Harness and Wilson 2001, APLIC 2006). The ratio of taps to other pole types was a rough measure of pole density, and in the ROF 1 of every 6 poles was a tap. Overall, .50% of poles were in high-risk categories (K. Winder, unpublished data).

The western Uintah Basin (hereafter, Uintah Basin) extended 79 km across northeastern Utah and, like the ROF, was developed for oil and gas production; however, agriculture (irrigated cropland and pasture) and tourism were also important industries. Distribution lines in the Uintah Basin serviced numerous farms and ranches, small communities, oil fields, and other businesses. Power lines often followed county roads and state highways, producing a 1.6 3 1.6-km (1.0 3 1.0-mile) grid across much of the region (Fig. 1). As a result, pole densities in the Uintah Basin were lower than those in the ROF (1 in 8 poles was a tap in Uintah Basin), and fewer poles (30%) were classified as high-risk structures. Of 210 mortalities recorded before our study, 49 (23%) were from the Uintah Basin.

The High Desert encompassed all other areas served by Moon Lake (including the eastern Uintah Basin) and was mostly rural and undeveloped. Distribution lines linked widely scattered ranches, small communities, and other developments, and pole densities were correspondingly low (1 in 13 poles was a tap). Overall, 14% of poles were in highrisk categories, and 27 (13%) of mortalities reported before our study were from the High Desert.

## History of Raptor Protection Efforts

Moon Lake began retrofitting distribution poles on a caseby-case basis in the late 1990s, focusing on poles with known mortalities and modifying poles as new mortalities occurred. In 1999, Moon Lake began a systematic assessment of raptor mortalities within its service area and, in 2000, completed a comprehensive avian protection plan, outlining standards and priorities for large-scale retrofitting (Harness 2000a, b). Mortality assessments in 1999 included a survey of all distribution poles in the ROF (N 5 2,930). From 2000 to 2003, Moon Lake expanded its retrofitting efforts to include poles with evidence of raptor use (white wash, prey remains, castings), preferred poles (poles known to be used frequently, often on bluffs and ridge lines), poles near nests and known roosts, and most poles classified as high-risk structures (Fig. 2). By fall 2003, Moon Lake had

completed modifications to 7,424 distribution poles throughout its service area (13% of available poles), including 1,721 poles in the ROF (59% of those available).

## METHODS

## Estimating Electrocution Rates

We defined an electrocution as the death of a bird caused by electric current on a utility pole. To estimate electrocution

rates, we searched for dead birds at randomly selected poles and at all poles along randomly selected distribution-line segments (hereafter, line segments) throughout the Moon Lake study area (Table 1). Regional differences in network design and function suggested that risk levels for raptors might also differ within the study area, so we conducted mortality surveys independently within the ROF, Uintah Basin, and High Desert. We assumed that risk levels for

raptors would vary within the 3 regions along a gradient based on pole densities, proportions of poles in high-risk categories, and other network features. We expected rates to be high in the ROF, low in the High Desert, and intermediate in the Uintah Basin.

In the ROF, we selected a simple, random sample of poles for monitoring because a highly clustered arrangement of poles and many short feeder lines (Fig. 3) suggested that linear sampling might not produce an unbiased sample. Many tap and dead-end poles were positioned at the beginning and end of feeder lines that were ,0.5 km long; thus, selection of long segments may have biased our samples toward tangents (poles forming straight lines), and selection of short segments may have favored taps and dead ends. In the ROF, .90% of poles were 3-phase structures, so we limited selections to these poles. During July 2001, we visited 615 preselected poles to remove old bird remains and to confirm that structures were properly classified. We eliminated 51 poles that were misclassified or that were disconnected from the power grid, leaving a sample of 564 poles for monitoring.

In the Uintah Basin and High Desert, we monitored line segments (2 km and 5 km, respectively) because lower pole densities and longer line configurations on the ground were conducive to linear sampling (Fig. 1). In both regions, we selected segments from 1-phase and 3-phase distribution lines in proportion to their occurrence (we ignored 2-phase lines because they were uncommon). We selected 10 1- phase and 20 3-phase segments in the Uintah Basin and 10 1-phase and 15 3-phase segments in the High Desert (Table 1). During an initial visit at each segment, we chose poles to represent start and end points and removed old bird remains from below poles. We rejected the site if access was denied by landowners or if the segment was disconnected from the power grid. We replaced rejected segments with additional randomly selected 2-km or 5-km segments.

From September 2001 to May 2003, we sampled most randomly selected line segments in the Uintah Basin and High Desert and all preselected poles in the ROF at intervals of 3–4 months. Some line segments were accessible for only part of the year because of snow conditions and were surveyed every 4–7 months. In all regions, we conducted surveys by truck or from an all-terrain vehicle and, occasionally, on foot if access was limited by road or weather conditions. Search areas around poles consisted of a circular plot with a 10-m radius centered on the pole. At each pole, we collected remains of all dead raptors and common ravens, identified carcasses to species and age class (ad, subadult) when possible, or assigned remains to 1 of 4 species groups (eagle, hawk, owl, or unclassified raptor). We included ravens in our samples because they are morphologically and behaviorally similar to raptors and often appear in electrocution data (APLIC 2006).

Long intervals between surveys were necessary because of the large number of segments and poles we monitored and because sampling was done across a 2-state area (Fig. 1). As a result, most of the dead birds we found during random surveys were in advanced stages of decay, and, after nearly 2

years of effort, our samples included few dead birds for which cause of death was known (see Results). However, sampling data suggested mortality levels in the ROF were substantially higher than in other regions. To increase sample sizes of dead birds suitable for necropsy and to improve precision in rate estimates, we discontinued random sampling in all regions in May 2003 and initiated monthly surveys of all poles in the ROF (Table 1). During August 2003, we removed all bird remains from the ROF, and from September 2003 to August 2004, we surveyed all poles to count and recover new mortalities, following the same search protocols we used during random sampling.

We estimated annual electrocution rates (deaths/pole/yr) for the ROF, Uintah Basin, and High Desert by totaling the number of mortalities found at randomly selected poles and line segments from 2001 to 2003 and dividing the total in each case by the number of poles sampled and the mean sampling period (Table 1). The mean sampling period was the average number of days between first and last visits at all sampling sites expressed in years. Because we could not assign a cause of death for most birds, samples from all 3 regions may have included some birds that died of causes other than electrocution (e.g., shooting or other trauma). Thus, the rate we calculated was the maximum estimate.

To estimate annual electrocution rates (deaths/pole/yr) for the ROF in 2003–2004, we totaled the number of mortalities we found during the 12 monthly surveys, along with mortalities reported to us by Moon Lake and subsequently recovered, and increased counts by the amount necessary to correct for scavenging effects (described below). We then divided the adjusted totals by the number of poles we surveyed each month (N 5 2,930). We estimated minimum rates as the corrected sum of confirmed electrocutions only. We estimated maximum rates as the corrected sum of all confirmed electrocutions and all mortalities for which we could not determine the cause of death (we did not include confirmed victims of shooting and birds killed in power-line collisions). We assumed that an unknown number of unclassified mortalities were electrocutions; thus, actual electrocution rates presumably fell between the minimum and maximum estimates.

## Necropsies

Because errors in assigning cause of death can influence the accuracy of electrocution mortality estimates, we attempted to determine cause of death for all fresh and relatively fresh birds we recovered (Ellis and Murphy 1969, Kroodsma 1978, Olson 2002). We conducted necropsies from April 2002 to July 2005 with assistance from pathologists at the Veterinary Teaching Hospital and Veterinary Diagnostics Laboratory, Colorado State University (Fort Collins, CO, USA). During necropsies, we obtained x-rays from most birds to assess evidence of shooting and examined carcasses for burns and other external signs of trauma. We examined birds that were not in advanced stages of decay for signs of internal abnormality or injury (e.g., hemorrhaging). We removed

livers and kidneys to assess lead and mercury concentrations because heavy metals may affect vision and motor skills in raptors and may increase electrocution risk for an affected bird (Gilsleider and Oehme 1982, Deem 1999). We did not necropsy skeletal remains but did collect and inspect these birds visually for signs of burns.

We classified carcasses showing burning and scorching of feathers, skin, bone, or other tissues as electrocutions. We classified birds with other injuries (e.g., external abrasions, bone fractures, internal hemorrhaging) but no burns as trauma victims (cause unknown). We classified carcasses showing bullet fragments, shotgun pellets, linear shattering of bones in x-rays, or sheering of feathers as shootings. We classified dead birds found between poles and near, or below, conductors that showed evidence of impact trauma (frontal abrasions, broken necks or wings) as power-line collisions. We classified birds showing no burns and no apparent injuries with lead and mercury concentrations below toxic levels as unknowns (cause of death not determined).

## Estimating Scavenger Effects

Potential sources of bias in estimating power-line mortality include crippling (escape of birds not killed immediately by electrocution or other trauma) and scavenging (removal of carcasses by predators or scavengers between searches; Bevanger 1999). The importance of crippling bias in electrocution studies is not well understood, but crippling rates may be higher for some raptors than was previously assumed (Dwyer 2006). We could not estimate crippling rates, but we did estimate scavenging effects by conducting carcass-removal experiments in the ROF using the dead raptors we found or raptors we obtained from the United States Fish and Wildlife Service. We placed dead raptors on the ground at randomly assigned distances (1 m, 2–4 m, 5– 9 m, 10–25 m) and directions (N, NE, E, SE, etc.) from randomly selected poles. On 26 June 2002, we placed 6 golden eagles below poles, and on 2–3 November 2002, we placed 21 golden eagles, 2 bald eagles (Haliaeetus leucocephalus), and 18 hawks and owls (Accipiter, Asio, Bubo, Buteo, and Circus spp.) below poles. We monitored carcasses daily for the first week and every 3–5 days thereafter until they disappeared or decayed beyond usability (i.e., until only feathers and bones remained).

Because we performed mortality surveys in the ROF at 1- month intervals in 2003–2004, we estimated correction factors for scavenging as the percentage of birds removed during the first 30 days of monitoring. Removal rates varied seasonally and by taxonomic group, and in the case of eagles, the sample sizes of birds placed below poles in June 2002 versus November 2002 differed substantially (6 vs. 23 birds were deployed); thus, we calculated one correction factor for eagles and a separate one for hawks and owls. We estimated the correction for eagles as the weighted mean of the 2 seasonal rates, weighted by the sample size in each case (Zar 1999). We calculated the carcass removal adjustment for hawks and owls as the percentage of birds removed during the November 2002 trial.

## Assessing Mortality Before and After Retrofitting in the ROF

In the ROF, we compared mortality rates from a survey of carcasses conducted at all distribution poles in 1999 (Harness 2000a) to our monthly pole surveys in the ROF from 2003 to 2004. Because the timing and methods of the 2 studies differed, we recalculated rate estimates for 2003– 2004 without adjusting for carcass removal by scavengers and compared maximum (but not minimum) rates for both studies. These steps were necessary because Harness (2000a) did not estimate scavenging rates in 1999 or conduct necropsies to confirm cause of death (precluding a min. rate estimate based on electrocuted birds alone). Harness (2000a) also conducted a single survey of all distribution poles (N 5 2,930) during a period of 4 months (Jun, Aug, Sep, Oct), but we conducted monthly surveys at all distribution poles during a 1-year period (Sep 2003 to Aug 2004). To develop comparable estimates for the 2 studies, we calculated a rate from our data using only mortalities that occurred in September–October 2003 and June–August 2004 and compared that with the rate we calculated from the 1999 data for the same 4 months. To calculate a rate for 1999, we reviewed the original mortality records and examined photographs of some dead birds taken in 1999 (not all birds were photographed) and classified each bird as a survey or presurvey mortality based on carcass condition and age. We classified carcasses that Harness (2000a) recorded as fresh, recent, or decayed as survey mortalities. We classified remains consisting of bones and feathers as survey mortalities only if the species or age class of the bird was recorded (we assumed that prolonged weathering had not occurred if these features were discernable). We classified carcasses that Harness (2000a) described specifically as old as presurvey mortalities.

## Estimating Raptor Densities

To assess whether a change in electrocution rates after retrofitting was related to changes in raptor densities through time, we counted perched raptors in the ROF along a standardized motor route (hereafter, the transect; Fig. 3) once each month from August 2001 to July 2004 (we did not survey in Mar 2002 or Jun–Jul 2003). We used distance sampling to estimate mean annual density (Rosenstock et al. 2002). We configured the transect, which was of unlimited width, to 1) ensure coverage of approximately 30% of the distribution poles and transmission towers in the ROF, 2) equalize coverage in its east and west halves, and 3) allow a survey period of 4– 5 hours. Thus, it was not randomly configured. During surveys, we drove ,20 km/hour, and 1–2 observers scanned for perched raptors. When we observed a perched bird (with the unaided eye), we used binoculars to determine species and age class. Moon Lake provided us with coordinates for all poles in its service area, and we estimated the perpendicular distance of each perched bird to the survey route with the Proximity and Near tools in ArcMap (Version 9.2).

We modeled raptor densities using the program DISTANCE (Version 5.0, Release 5; Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment, University of St. Andrews,

We multiplied the transect length by the number of visits to increase precision in density estimates and excluded the 10% of observations that occurred farthest from the transect to improve model fit (see Buckland et al. 2001 for methods of truncating observations at extreme distances). We used a monotonic, decreasing key function (half-normal, uniform, hazard rate or negative exponential) with possible cosine or polynomial adjustment terms on pooled data to model the detection function and to obtain an estimate of P, the proportion of individuals detected along the transect. We assessed model fit using Kolmogorov–Smirnov goodness-of-fit (GOF) tests and selected the best fitting models using Akaike’s Information Criterion adjusted for small sample size (AICc; Buckland et al. 2001, Burnham and Anderson 2002). Because we only collected data from one transect, we could not use the preferred bootstrap method of variance estimation. Therefore, we report the theoretical variance multiplied by 2 to account for potential violation of the assumption that the data have a Poisson distribution (Buckland et al. 2001). Because of the lack of spatial replication, our inference space is limited to the surveyed area.

## Data Analysis

Except for DISTANCE analyses, we ran all statistical tests using SAS software (SAS/STAT Version 9.1; SAS Institute, Cary, NC) and set a 5 0.05 for hypothesis tests comparing differences among 2 or more samples. We used 2 3 2 contingency table analysis and the likelihood ratio chi-square (G-test of independence; PROC FREQ in SAS) to evaluate differences in scavenging rates among groups of species (eagles and other raptors). We evaluated annual variation in estimated raptor densities as the degree of overlap of 95% confidence intervals. We interpreted lack of overlap of confidence intervals with means of other estimates as evidence for statistical difference between estimates, whereas we interpreted asymmetrical overlap of means (intervals overlapped one mean but not the other) as suggestive of a statistical difference between groups (Ramsey and Schafer 2002).

## Carcass Removal Trials in the ROF

Of the 6 golden eagles we placed below poles in June 2002, one disappeared on day 15 and another disappeared on day 26 (a 33% monthly removal rate), but none of the 21 golden eagles and 2 bald eagles we placed the following November were removed. We estimated a mean removal rate of 6.8% per month for eagles in the ROF. In contrast, 13 of 18 hawks and owls that we placed under poles in November 2002 were removed during the 38-day period, a significantly higher removal rate (72%) than we observed for golden eagles (G1 5 22.80, P , 0.001). Ten of these birds were taken during the first 30 days (the interval between carcass surveys in 2003–2004), giving a correction factor of 55.6% for adjusting-rate estimates (10/18 5 0.556).

## Electrocution Rates

To compare electrocution rates among regions, we used 14 birds found at 3-phase poles during random sampling (9 from the ROF, 2 from the Uintah Basin, and 3 from the High Desert). We did not use 2 birds that died of causes other than electrocution. Each transect in each region was sampled at an average rate of 1.42 years (ROF), 1.35 years (Uintah Basin), and 1.05 years (High Desert), and we sampled 564 (ROF), 411 (Uintah Basin), and 633 (High Desert) poles. Thus, mortality in the ROF (9/564/1.42 5 0.0112 deaths/pole/ yr) was 2.5–3.0 times higher than the Uintah Basin (0.0036 deaths/pole/yr) and High Desert (0.0045 deaths/pole/yr). We found no mortalities at 1-phase distribution poles during random sampling.

We estimated minimum annual electrocution rates using 15 electrocuted birds from the ROF in 2003–2004 (Table 3), and we estimated maximum annual electrocution rates using 30 birds, which represented nearly all mortalities that we recorded (Table 4). In maximum-rate estimates, we included 24 of 26 birds we found and 6 birds reported by study cooperators; we did not use a bird that was shot and a bird killed in a power-line collision. We adjusted these counts for scavenging effects (increased eagle counts by 0.068 and counts of other species by 0.556), and, based on

the minimum and maximum rates, estimated that 18–38 raptors and ravens were electrocuted in the ROF from September 2003 to August 2004, which is 0.006–0.013 birds/pole/year (e.g., 0.006 birds/pole/yr 3 2,930 poles 5 18.46 birds/yr). Minimum rates for eagles were slightly higher than those for other raptor species, but maximum rates were nearly the same for the 2 groups (Table 4). Of 15 confirmed electrocutions in the ROF, 13 occurred on 3- phase distribution poles, one on an H-frame transmission tower, and one at a substation. Of the 13 birds killed on distribution poles, we found 10 (77%) below poles classified as high-risk structures (taps, dead ends, and equipment poles), and we recovered 3 below simple tangents (i.e., configured with conductors and a neutral wire only).

## Mortality Before and After Retrofitting in the ROF

We classified 44 of 61 mortalities recorded during a survey of distribution poles in 1999 (Harness 2000a) as presurvey mortalities and excluded them from rate estimates. We used the remaining 17 mortalities recorded during June, August, September, and October 1999 to estimate a baseline electrocution rate of 0.0058 deaths/pole for the 4 months (17 deaths/2,930 poles 5 0.0058 deaths/pole). We used 9 mortalities counted during the same months in 2003 to 2004 to estimate a comparable rate of 0.0031 deaths/pole, a 47% decrease from 1999 to 2004.

## Raptor Densities in the ROF

During 33 monthly surveys conducted from August 2001 to July 2004, we counted 184 raptors perched on distribution poles and transmission towers in the ROF (Table 5). Monthly counts ranged from 0–20 birds (x ̄ 5 5.4). Golden eagles comprised 60% of all detections averaged over 3 years, followed by bald eagles, red-tailed hawks, and ferruginous hawks (Buteo regalis).

We fit detection functions, which varied by year, to our data (GOF tests, Ps . 0.45; Table 5). Top models consisted of half-normal, uniform, and negative exponential detection functions with 5 cosine and polynomial series expansion terms. Asymmetrical overlap in 95% confidence intervals suggests that P in 2003–2004 was also higher than P in 2001–2002. ## DISCUSSION

Mortalities documented by Moon Lake before our study strongly implicated the ROF as a primary source of raptor electrocutions and suggested a level of mortality that was out of proportion to the number of poles in service. As a result, Moon Lake focused much of its retrofitting effort in the ROF, ultimately modifying nearly 60% of poles in that area. Data collected from 2001 to 2003 confirmed the importance of the ROF as the primary source of raptor mortality on the Moon Lake system. The ROF accounted for 59% of mortalities in our random sampling data and, as predicted, had the highest electrocution rates in the study area. However, rates were lowest in the Uintah Basin, not the High Desert as we predicted.

High mortality levels in the ROF were influenced by the area’s conspicuously high pole densities and the large proportion of poles in high-risk categories (.50%, compared with 30% and 14% in the Uintah Basin and High Desert, respectively). High pole densities may have increased raptor use by attracting birds from areas with fewer perches, which included most landscapes within 40 km of the ROF. The large proportion of poles in high-risk categories (taps, dead-end units, and equipment poles) ensured that every bird in the ROF had a 1:2 chance of encountering a high-risk pole.

Other factors may have influenced mortality levels in the ROF, including consistent use of the area by golden eagles and high prey availability. Golden eagles are common residents of northwestern Colorado (Andrews and Righter 1992), and some pairs probably bred in the vicinity of the ROF. We observed golden eagles on ROF power poles during nearly every perch survey from 2001 to 2004, and across all surveys, the species accounted for 60% of birds observed. We did not collect data on prey populations, but prey availability, like pole density, may have attracted birds to the ROF from surrounding areas. We observed white-tailed prairie dogs (Cynomys leucurus) almost daily, and pronghorn antelope

Electrocution rates in the Uintah Basin and High Desert may have been influenced more by landscape factors that affected raptor population densities and perch availability than by network design factors. Shrub–steppe vegetation dominated most landscapes in the High Desert, and power poles often were the most prevalent structures available for perching. In comparison, natural perches were relatively abundant in the Uintah Basin because of its pastoral setting. The High Desert also had lower levels of development than the Uintah Basin and, we assume, lower disturbance levels. As a result, raptor densities may have been higher in the High Desert than in the Uintah Basin. The overall effect of these differences may have been a higher dependence on power poles by comparatively more birds, and thus higher electrocution rates, in the High Desert.

Shortening intervals between surveys during carcass searches in the ROF (2003–2004) nearly tripled the proportion of fresh or relatively fresh birds we recovered but did not improve the proportion of birds for which cause of death was known. Electrocutions are identified by burning and charring of tissue and feathers, but burns are not always present or obvious on electrocution victims (Thomas 1999, Schomburg 2003). More than 40% of birds recovered in the ROF in 2003–2004 showed no signs of burns, illness, trauma, or contamination. Unfortunately, there are no known histologic or serologic markers of electrocution for raptors (T. Spraker, Veterinary Teaching Hospital, Colorado State University, personal communication), and the proportion of electrocutions lacking visible burns in a sample has never been estimated. It might have been possible to reduce the number of unknowns by testing for additional environmental toxicants (we evaluated only lead and mercury), but the cost of testing for potentially dozens of substances was prohibitive and may have produced no new information.

Because many birds that we collected during monthly surveys in the ROF lacked a cause of death, we did not calculate a mean death rate or standard error and confidence limits for any of our samples. Calculating a mean for these samples would have required that we assign unknowns (birds with no cause of death) to mortality classes arbitrarily or eliminate .40% of our data. Instead, we set lower and upper limits for possible values of the actual rate. Adjusting these estimates for scavenger effects increased the likelihood that intervals between estimates contained the actual rates.

In some raptor mortality studies, researchers used surrogate species (e.g., domestic chickens or game hens) to estimate scavenger effects; however, Smallwood (2007) found that these birds were removed by scavengers 10–20 times faster than small- and large-bodied raptors. We do not recommend the use of surrogates for this purpose but acknowledge that availability of freshly killed raptors may be a limiting factor in carcass removal studies. We obtained enough raptor carcasses to assess scavenging rates only in the ROF.

Other potential sources of error, including habitat bias (missing carcasses because of habitat factors such as dense vegetation) and search bias (overlooking some carcasses within a search area), were probably negligible. These biases were not important because we searched within restricted and well-defined areas (below poles) in a desert environment, and in principle, all poles were accessible, and all birds were recoverable (unless they were removed by scavengers). We did not measure crippling rates, but on 2 occasions, we found injured birds (a red-tailed hawk and a golden eagle) that were victims of electric shock (both showed burns on feathers or feet). However, we conducted .45,000 searches at distribution poles and encountered only these 2 live birds. Thus, we assume crippling bias was a negligible influence on our estimates.

Estimates of scavenger effects revealed that hawks and owls were underrepresented in our raw mortality data because they were removed by scavengers at substantially higher rates than eagles (55.6% vs. 6.8%). Adjustment of electrocution rates to compensate for the difference showed that mortality for the 2 groups was similar. This suggests that hawks and owls in the ROF were as likely to be electrocuted as eagles in spite of inherent size differences. The lack of an effect here may be related to the large number of high-risk poles in the ROF. One of every 2 poles was a tap, dead end, or equipment pole, and all of these poles shared the critical risk factor of reduced clearances among electrical components. Large numbers of poles in high-risk categories may have contributed to unusually high mortality rates for a species group (hawks and owls) that, in other settings, would be killed relatively less often. Similar rates among species groups did not equate to similar rates among species, however. If we had considered mortality separately for each species, electrocution rates for golden eagles would have been substantially higher than rates for other species for the simple reason that the eagle group included only golden eagles and the hawk–owl group included multiple species. We have no information on the origin of golden eagles found dead in the ROF, nor do we have any information on local population size, so we cannot determine the effect of these rates on the local population. However, given continuing efforts by Moon Lake to reduce electrocution rates by retrofitting poles, we would not expect to see substantial population effects on golden eagles in the future as a direct consequence of power-line electrocutions.

Our results suggest that the retrofitting conducted by Moon Lake substantially reduced electrocution mortality; however, interpretation of these results was complicated by

several factors. First, our use of mortality data from an earlier study (Harness 2000a) was retrospective, and we made somewhat arbitrary decisions to include or exclude birds from 1999 in the rate estimates based on notes about carcass condition in the original mortality records, sometimes aided by photographs of dead birds taken in 1999. We removed old bird remains from sampling sites before our surveys to ensure that all birds included in rate estimates died during the sampling period. This could not be done retrospectively, and as a result, we may have included birds in the 1999 estimate that were killed before the Harness (2000a) surveys, or we may have excluded birds that should have been part of the mortality sample. Second, no measure of raptor density or abundance for 1999 was available, and we cannot be sure that numbers of birds using the oil field during the earlier survey were similar to those in 2003–2004. Although our density estimates suggest the rate reduction was not an artifact of a decreasing raptor population during our study, we can infer nothing about raptor abundance in 1999 from our data.

The possibility that we overestimated mortality in 1999 or that higher raptor density in 1999 was responsible for at least part of the rate reduction we measured was offset by 2 factors. First, we were conservative in assigning mortalities in 1999 to the data set used in rate estimates. We included just 17 of 61 mortalities documented in 1999. Second, we sampled poles more often in 2003–2004 than Harness did in 1999. We checked each pole 4 times, and Harness (2000a) checked each pole once during equivalent sampling periods. If Harness (2000a) had checked every pole as often as we did, it is likely that additional mortalities would have been found in 1999. Thus, the 47% reduction we estimated may have been conservative.

Estimates of mortality from the ROF in 2003 to 2004 were lower than all comparable estimates (expressed as deaths/pole/yr) we found in the literature (Table 7). Minimum and maximum electrocution rates from a study in southwestern Idaho (R. N. Lehman, United States Geological Survey, unpublished data) were slightly higher than in our study, but researchers in Mexico (Cartron et al. 2005) reported mortality levels .20 times higher than those we reported. The highest rate (0.3549 deaths/pole/yr) was from Don ̃ana National Park and surrounding areas in southwestern Spain before an extensive retrofitting effort (Ferrer et al. 1991; Janss and Ferrer 1999b, 2001). However, interpretation of these and other estimates were complicated by physical differences among study areas and differences in the methods used to collect and analyze mortality and scavenging data. For example, Platt (2005) used methods similar to ours to estimate minimum and maximum electrocution rates in an area with retrofitting levels similar to those we observed, but used domestic chickens (Gallicus domesticus), not raptors, to measure scavenging effects. To determine actual removal rates, Cartron et al. (2005) left some dead raptors below poles where they were found, but worked with unretrofitted utility structures. Utility structures made of steel are self-grounded and require just one contact with an energized conductor to be lethal. In Europe, nearly all utility structures are in this class, and all birds that use them, including small birds, are at risk. Most poles in the United States are made of wood (usually a nonconductive material), and 2 points of contact on these structures are necessary for electrocutions to occur (Harness 2001, APLIC 2006). As a result, most electrocutions in the United States involve relatively large birds (i.e., raptors), and overall rates are likely to be lower.

## MANAGEMENT IMPLICATIONS

Power companies may have the greatest effect on raptor safety by implementing large-scale monitoring programs to provide baseline information on power-line hazards and mortality and focusing subsequent mitigation efforts on poles and in habitats that pose the greatest risk to the greatest number of birds. Utilities need to balance the goal of monitoring at more than one scale with the need for reliable and comparable rate estimates before and after retrofitting. Rate estimates should be based on probability sampling in some form and should incorporate spatial and temporal elements (e.g., deaths/pole/yr). Search intervals to recover dead birds should be as short as possible and, ideally, the same before and after retrofitting. Utilities should consider all birds found below power poles as electrocutions and should use maximum rates as benchmarks for monitoring. Minimum rates should be estimated only if carcasses are recovered and necropsied, but carcasses cannot be recovered without state and federal salvage permits. Birds that cannot be recovered should be marked to avoid double

counting and birds killed before sampling should not be used in rate estimates. The ability to address biasing factors is likely to be low for most utilities, but known biases can be balanced across all samples to ensure valid comparisons. Precision of rate estimates in future studies will be improved if fresh raptor carcasses for use in carcass removal trials become more available and if necropsies produce fewer unknowns. Refining retrofitting techniques after each management action and retrofitting poles as new mortalities occur will produce additional rate reductions. Utilities also need to incorporate raptor-friendly design standards in all new power-line constructions. We doubt that raptor electrocutions can be eliminated completely, no matter how much effort and expense are invested. A reasonable goal is to minimize electrocutions so that population effects are minimized. Raptor densities should be estimated when possible, to clarify relationships between retrofitting and observed rate reductions, but should not be used to infer population effects resulting from electrocutions or efforts to minimize electrocutions.
